title: The mechanism of the psychophysiological effects of placebo.
abstract: The psychological and physiological components of the placebo phenomenon are connected in a way which is analogous to the connection between thermal imagery and skin blood flow and skin temperature. The content of mental imagery affects specifically skin blood flow and causes temperature changes. By analogy, the physiological effects of placebo depend on the content of the patient's treatment-related imagery. The long term effects of placebo in a specific disease depend on the duration and repetition of a single placebo effect. Placebo affects through a complicated and holistic psychophysiological system. Therefore its effect can be more long-lasting than the effects of more specific agents. Thus placebo should be used intentionally together with treatments and drugs which have more direct physiological and pharmacological effects.

screening.rationale: The paper is a theoretical/hypothesis article whose explicit focus is mechanisms of the placebo phenomenon (placebo science), meeting inclusion for conceptual/theory work on placebo.

classification.summary: Proposes that placebo effects arise from treatment-related mental imagery producing specific psychophysiological changes (e.g., skin blood flow and temperature), potentially producing long-lasting effects and useful adjunctive roles for placebo.

title: Placebo response in depression: a search for predictors.
abstract: Although 30-40% of depressed patients respond to placebo treatment, few predictors of placebo response have been identified. We evaluated patients with moderate to severe depression who had received placebo for 3-6 weeks in multicenter clinical trials (Study 1, n = 125; Study 2, n = 88). Placebo response rates (greater than 50% improvement in Hamilton total depression score) were 38.4% and 30.7%, respectively. Despite differences in treatment outcome, baseline clinical and demographic characteristics were similar for responders and nonresponders. The studies confirmed the substantial placebo response in moderately to severely depressed patients and suggested chronicity may be a predictor.

screening.rationale: Secondary analysis focused on placebo-arm responses and predictors across antidepressant RCTs, making placebo response the analytic object (inclusion rule 2).

classification.summary: Analyzed placebo arms from two multicenter antidepressant trials (n=125 and n=88) and found substantial placebo response rates (38.4% and 30.7%), with longer chronicity suggested as a predictor.
classification.key_finding: Found placebo response rates of 38.4% and 30.7% in two trials and suggested greater chronicity predicted lower placebo response.

title: Experimenter demands in the balanced-placebo design: reply to Collins and Searles.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly discusses experimenter demands in the balanced-placebo design (a placebo/expectation methodology), so it is a commentary on placebo research methodology.

classification.summary: Was a reply/commentary addressing experimenter demand characteristics in the balanced-placebo design and methodological implications for alcohol/behavior research.

title: Alcohol and the balanced-placebo design: were experimenter demands in expectancy really tested? Comment on Knight, Barbaree, and Boland (1986).

screening.rationale: Commentary focused on the balanced-placebo design and whether experimenter demand effects in expectancy (a placebo/expectation methodology issue) were tested, making placebo/expectation methodology the paper's subject.

classification.summary: Commented on whether experimenter demand confounded expectancy tests in balanced-placebo alcohol experiments and critiqued the methodology.

title: Placebo response in panic disorder.
abstract: Of 43 patients with panic disorder or agoraphobia with panic attacks who took placebo for 8 weeks in two double-blind studies, one in four markedly improved. Those with consistently normal dexamethasone suppression test results were significantly more likely to show a placebo response as were those with lower anxiety ratings at the outset of treatment.

screening.rationale: Paper analyzed outcomes and predictors within placebo-treated patients (placebo response was the analytic focus across placebo arms).

classification.summary: Analyzed 43 patients assigned to placebo across two double-blind trials for panic disorder and reported that one-quarter markedly improved and that normal dexamethasone suppression and lower baseline anxiety predicted placebo response.
classification.key_finding: About 25% of placebo-treated patients markedly improved; normal dexamethasone suppression test results and lower baseline anxiety were associated with greater placebo response.

title: Placebos and common factors in two decades of psychotherapy research.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose explicit subject is placebos and common (nonspecific) factors in psychotherapy across two decades, meeting inclusion as a review of placebo-related phenomena.

classification.summary: Reviews two decades of psychotherapy research on placebos and common factors, synthesizing how nonspecific processes contribute to therapeutic change.

title: Dr. Xz, the placebo.
journal: Iowa medicine : journal of the Iowa Medical Society

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and title plus MeSH terms are insufficient to determine whether placebo phenomena were the paper's explicit focus.

classification.summary: No abstract or full text available; insufficient information to judge whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were the paper's focus.

title: The acute effect of an oral "inotropic" placebo on the exercise capacity of patients with chronic cardiac failure.
abstract: Uncontrolled studies have suggested that the newer oral phosphodiesterase inhibitors milrinone and enoximone acutely improve exercise performance in patients with severe chronic cardiac failure. To determine whether an oral placebo presented as an inotropic agent could acutely enhance exercise capacity, two separate groups of stable heart failure patients were studied by serial exercise testing and respiratory gas exchange analysis. Group 1 had nine patients studied four hours after a single oral dose of placebo, and group 2 had ten patients retested after one to two weeks of placebo therapy. No significant change was seen in the mean exercise time, mean peak oxygen consumption, and the mean oxygen consumption at anaerobic threshold after placebo administration in both group 1 and group 2 patients. Improvements in exercise time, peak oxygen consumption, and oxygen consumption at anaerobic threshold occurred in five patients in group 1 and seven patients in group 2. The improvements exceeded the baseline variability of 10 percent in three group 1 patients. Among group 2 patients, the increase in exercise time, peak oxygen consumption, and oxygen consumption at anaerobic threshold exceeded 10 percent in six, four, and four patients, respectively. Thus, stable chronic heart failure patients can achieve a true baseline exercise capacity. Small improvements in exercise performance seen acutely after oral inotropic drug therapy in individual heart failure patients must be interpreted with caution, as they may be due to a placebo effect.

screening.rationale: Study's stated aim was to test whether an oral placebo presented as an inotropic agent could acutely enhance exercise capacity, directly studying placebo response/effect.

classification.summary: Tested whether an oral placebo described as an inotropic drug acutely improved exercise capacity in 19 stable chronic heart failure patients and found no significant mean change, though some individuals showed >10% improvements.
classification.key_finding: No significant group-level change in exercise time or peak VO2, but several individual patients showed improvements exceeding baseline variability.

title: The placebo effect in agoraphobia--II.
journal: The Journal of nervous and mental disease
abstract: Analyses in 44 agoraphobic patients given single-blind placebo over a two-week period, without the customary confound of instructions of exposure to phobic situations, replicated previous findings of a weak placebo response in that there were statistically, but not clinically, significant reductions in panic and phobic symptoms. Further analyses of a representative subsample of 10 patients who continued to receive placebo revealed that the placebo response was maintained and even increased at the end of 10 weeks when 20% to 30% of the patients could be classified as marked responders on key panic and phobic measures. Results also revealed an interesting observation that most of the improvement in panic, anxiety, and depression occurred early whereas improvement in phobic measures was more gradual and increased significantly over time. Implications for clinical research are briefly discussed.

screening.rationale: Primary analysis focused on the magnitude and time course of placebo response in agoraphobic patients given single‑blind placebo (placebo response as object of study).

classification.summary: Found that single‑blind placebo produced small statistically significant reductions in panic and phobic symptoms in 44 agoraphobic patients, with 20–30% classified as marked responders after 10 weeks and phobic improvement increasing over time.
classification.key_finding: Small but statistically significant early reductions in panic/anxiety; 20–30% were marked responders by 10 weeks, with phobic measures improving gradually.

title: Controlled treatment trials in the irritable bowel syndrome: a critique.
abstract: The irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common and poorly understood chronic condition that is treated with a great variety of drugs and other therapies without notable enduring success. As there are no objective markers of improvement, and because there may be a very large placebo response, potential treatments for IBS are difficult to assess. Probably the only method that can reliably evaluate IBS therapies is the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled treatment trial. The purpose of this review is to critically examine issues central to establishing the efficacy of treatments for IBS in such trials. These include the definition of IBS, measures of efficacy, the placebo response, trial length, maintaining blindedness, the crossover design, ability to generalize, and statistical considerations. With this background, all published IBS treatment trials are examined. It is concluded that not a single study offers convincing evidence that any therapy is effective in treating the IBS symptom complex. Well-designed and executed IBS treatment trials are urgently needed; suggestions are given for essential features of such trials.

screening.rationale: Review critically examined trial methodology with placebo response and related issues as a central focus.

classification.summary: Reviewed randomized, placebo-controlled IBS treatment trials, critiqued methodology and emphasized large placebo responses and design limitations, concluding no convincing therapy existed.

title: The effect of nasal flow on breathlessness in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
journal: The American review of respiratory disease
abstract: Many patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) receiving supplemental oxygen state that this treatment makes them less short of breath at rest. We postulated that this phenomenon may be related to improved arterial oxygenation, reduced ventilation, or stimulation of nasal receptors caused by the flow of gas. Eight patients who reported this phenomenon were studied in a quiet room. Each patient received zero flow, 2, or 4 L/min of air or oxygen through nasal cannula for 5 min at each level in random order in a single blind manner. At the end of each period, arterial blood gas composition was measured, and breathlessness was assessed with a visual analog scale. The scale was calibrated to read from zero (not at all breathless) to 100 (extremely short of breath). The entire protocol was repeated after application of topical lidocaine to the nasal passages. Results were assessed by analysis of variance. We found no significant effect of inspired oxygen concentration, gas flow, arterial oxygen tension, or arterial carbon dioxide tension on breathlessness. There was, however, a significant increase in breathlessness after nasal anesthesia from 44 +/- 3 SEM to 52 +/- 4 SEM (p less than 0.005). We suggest that the reduction of breathlessness in these patients by nasal oxygen is a placebo effect caused by wearing the nasal cannulas and is unrelated to gas flow or the increased arterial oxygen tension.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly investigated whether symptom relief from nasal oxygen was due to oxygenation, airflow, or nasal receptor stimulation and concluded the effect was due to wearing cannulas (a contextual/placebo mechanism), with an experimental manipulation (nasal anesthesia) testing that mechanism.

classification.summary: Tested airflow and oxygen versus nasal receptor stimulation in 8 COPD patients and found nasal anesthesia increased breathlessness, suggesting symptom relief from nasal oxygen was due to wearing cannulas (contextual/placebo cue) rather than gas exchange.
classification.key_finding: Nasal anesthesia increased breathlessness from 44 ± 3 to 52 ± 4 on VAS (p < 0.005), implicating nasal sensory cues in perceived relief from supplemental oxygen.

title: Reduction of postoperative pain and swelling by ultrasound treatment: a placebo effect.
abstract: Ultrasound (US) therapy is used to reduce pain and inflammation and to accelerate healing after soft tissue injury. However, there is little objective evidence of its effectiveness and the mechanisms which may cause these effects are unknown. In a placebo-controlled double-blind clinical trial we examined the contribution of placebo and massage effects in ultrasound therapy following bilateral surgical extraction of lower third molars. Four to 6 h after surgery the patients (25 per group) received either no therapy, US (0.1 W/cm2), 'mock' US with massage, 'mock' US without massage, or 'self-massage' with a dummy applicator. Facial swelling, trismus, serum C-reactive protein, serum cortisol, pain and anxiety were measured 24 h postoperatively. The results showed that the beneficial analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of US therapy were placebo-mediated, with maximum effect in the placebo ('mock' US) group without circular massaging with the applicator). Self-massage by the patient produced no significant effect. This placebo action was independent of changes in serum cortisol or patient anxiety state. US therapy can significantly reduce postoperative morbidity, but by placebo-mediated mechanisms which are unrelated to the US itself.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that explicitly tested and attributed analgesic and anti-inflammatory outcomes to placebo (mock ultrasound) versus no treatment and real US, meeting the placebo-effect inclusion criterion (placebo-mediated effects isolated).

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial after third-molar extraction found that mock (placebo) ultrasound produced the largest reductions in postoperative pain and inflammation compared with no therapy or self-massage.
classification.key_finding: Mock (placebo) ultrasound without circular massaging produced the greatest analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects; self-massage had no significant effect (25 participants per group, N≈125).

title: Placebo effects in the treatment of male dating anxiety.
journal: Journal of behavior therapy and experimental psychiatry
abstract: The outcomes of cognitive-behavioral and high credibility placebo group treatments were compared in a sample of nineteen heterosocially anxious males. At post-test and at a 3-month follow-up, both treatments showed improvement on self-report measures of interpersonal functioning (ps less than 0.05). The cognitive-behavioral treatment showed a consistent pattern of improvement on self-report and behavioral measures of anxiety (ps less than 0.05), but, overall, the groups showed comparable levels of effectiveness. The possibility that both treatments relied on placebo mechanisms is discussed.

screening.rationale: A trial directly compared a cognitive-behavioral treatment with a high-credibility placebo group and reported placebo-group improvement, making placebo mechanisms a substantive focus of the study.

classification.summary: Compared cognitive-behavioral therapy to a high-credibility placebo group in 19 heterosocially anxious males and found both groups improved on self-report at post-test and 3-month follow-up, with CBT showing more consistent behavioral gains.
classification.key_finding: Both CBT and the high-credibility placebo group produced significant self-reported improvement; CBT produced greater behavioral anxiety improvements but groups were comparable overall.

title: Paranormal healing and hypertension.
abstract: A prospective randomised trial was carried out to see whether paranormal healing by laying on of hands might reduce blood pressure in essential hypertension and whether such an effect might be due to a paranormal, psychological, or placebo factor. Patients were randomised to three treatment groups: paranormal healing by laying on of hands (n = 40), paranormal healing at a distance (n = 37), and no paranormal healing (controls; n = 38). Healing at a distance and no paranormal healing were investigated double blind. Systolic and diastolic blood pressures were significantly reduced in all three groups at week 15 (mean reduction (95% confidence interval) 17.1 (14.0 to 20.2)/8.3 (6.6 to 10.0) mm Hg). Only the successive reductions in diastolic blood pressures among the groups from week to week were significantly different. Each week diastolic pressure was consistently lower (average 1.9 mm Hg) after healing at a distance compared with control, but on paired comparison these differences were not significant. Probably week to week variations among the groups accounted for any differences noted. In this study no treatment was consistently better than another and the data cannot therefore be taken as evidence of a paranormal effect on blood pressure. Probably the fall in blood pressure in all three groups either was caused by the psychosocial approach or was a placebo effect of the trial itself.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly tested paranormal healing versus no-healing and discussed whether observed BP falls were due to psychosocial or placebo factors, making placebo/ trial-related response a stated focus.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared laying-on-of-hands, distant healing, and no healing in essential hypertension and found blood pressure fell in all groups with no consistent treatment superiority, suggesting psychosocial or trial/placebo-related effects.
classification.key_finding: Blood pressure declined in all three groups with no treatment consistently better, implying the observed improvements likely reflected psychosocial or placebo/trial effects rather than a paranormal effect.

title: The nurse's ethical guide to placebo giving.

screening.rationale: Paper is explicitly about the ethics and guidance of placebo giving in nursing, so placebo is the main subject (placebo prescribing/ethics).

classification.summary: Provided ethical guidance and discussion for nurses on the practice of giving placebos in clinical care.

title: Relative contribution of specific and nonspecific treatment effects: meta-analysis of placebo-controlled behavior therapy research.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly states a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled behavior therapy research addressing specific versus nonspecific (placebo) effects, making placebo response/effects the paper's focus (meets inclusion criterion 4).

classification.summary: Meta-analyzed placebo-controlled behavior therapy studies and assessed the relative contributions of specific and nonspecific (placebo) treatment effects.

title: Biological differences in endogenous depressive placebo responders versus nonresponders: dexamethasone suppression test and sleep EEG data.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly compared biological differences between depressive placebo responders and nonresponders, making placebo response the study focus (placebo as object of study).

classification.summary: Compared dexamethasone suppression test and sleep EEG markers between depressive patients who responded to placebo and those who did not.

title: The placebo effect during a double blind trial of recombinant alpha 2 interferon in multiple sclerosis patients: immunological and clinical findings.
abstract: A double-blind, placebo controlled trial of recombinant alpha 2 interferon in relapsing/remitting multiple sclerosis patients was performed to assess the clinical and immunological responses to treatment. This study demonstrated that natural killer (NK) cell activity, known to be enhanced by interferon (IFN) treatment, increased during the first week of treatment in both the IFN and placebo treatment groups. After the first week of treatment NK cell activity returned to baseline levels in both groups, and subsequently declined in the IFN treatment group. Patients in both groups improved clinically, as evidenced by a reduction in the exacerbation rate. Furthermore, a similar incidence of adverse reactions to treatment were reported by both groups. The mechanism underlying the response to placebo is not known. However, it is unlikely that the long term clinical improvement (one year) in either group is related to the transient increase in NK cell activity.

screening.rationale: Title and abstract explicitly report and analyze placebo-group immunological and clinical responses within a double-blind RCT, making placebo response an object of study.

classification.summary: Reported that both interferon and placebo groups showed a transient increase in NK cell activity and clinical improvement (reduced exacerbation rate) during a double-blind RCT in relapsing-remitting MS patients.
classification.key_finding: Both treatment and placebo groups had a week-long increase in NK activity and comparable reductions in exacerbation rate, suggesting a notable placebo-associated immunological and clinical response.

title: Double-blind versus deceptive administration of a placebo.
abstract: Subjects were given varying doses of a placebo, consisting of decaffeinated coffee, with double-blind or deceptive instructions. Deceptive administration simulated clinical situations in that subjects were led to believe that they were receiving an active drug. In contrast, subjects in double-blind conditions were aware that they might receive a placebo. Double-blind and deceptive administration of the placebo produced different, and in some instances, opposite effects on pulse rate, systolic blood pressure, and subjective mood. Deceptive administration produced an increase in pulse rate, whereas double-blind administration did not. A theoretically predicted curvilinear effect on systolic blood pressure, alertness, tension, and certainty of having consumed caffeine was confirmed with deceptive administration, but not with double-blind administration. Double-blind administration produced curves in the opposite direction on each of these variables. The effects of the placebo on motor performance varied as a function of subject's beliefs about the effects of caffeine. These data challenge the validity of double-blind experimental designs and suggest that this common method of drug assessment may lead to spurious conclusions.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation contrasted deceptive (told-active) versus double-blind (uncertain) administration of an inert beverage to isolate placebo/context effects on physiology, mood, and performance.

classification.summary: Found that deceptive (told-active) versus double-blind administration of decaffeinated coffee produced different and sometimes opposite effects on pulse, systolic blood pressure, subjective mood, and motor performance.
classification.key_finding: Deceptive administration increased pulse and produced curvilinear effects on systolic blood pressure, alertness, tension, and certainty of having consumed caffeine, whereas double-blind administration did not or produced opposite curves.

title: Effect of placebo on meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion and serum gastrin concentration. Studies in healthy volunteers and duodenal ulcer patients.
abstract: The effect of placebos on gastric acid secretion in humans is unknown, even though placebo therapy is relatively effective in ulcer patients. Therefore, we evaluated the effect of a placebo capsule on meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion and serum gastrin concentrations in 10 healthy subjects and also in 10 patients with chronic duodenal ulcer. Each subject and patient was studied twice and in random order, once with placebo therapy prior to the meal and once without placebo. In either healthy subjects or duodenal ulcer patients, meal-stimulated acid secretion and serum gastrin concentrations were not significantly different with or without placebo administration. These studies demonstrate that a placebo capsule, administered by a physician just prior to a meal, has little, if any, effect on acid secretion or gastrin release in response to the meal. Any beneficial effects of placebos in treating patients with peptic ulcer disease are probably unrelated to inhibition of meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion.

screening.rationale: Within-subject randomized comparison of placebo capsule versus no placebo tested placebo effects on meal-stimulated gastric acid and gastrin, so placebo effect was the explicit experimental focus.

classification.summary: Randomized within-subject study tested a placebo capsule versus no placebo in 10 healthy volunteers and 10 duodenal ulcer patients and found no effect on meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion or serum gastrin.
classification.key_finding: Found no significant difference in meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion or serum gastrin with versus without placebo administration.

title: An integration of ethical and clinical considerations in the use of placebos.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper's primary focus is ethical and clinical issues of placebo use, fitting 'placebo_science_other' inclusion for reviews/commentary on placebo ethics.

classification.summary: Reviews ethical and clinical considerations in the use of placebos, with attention to disclosure, withholding treatment, and vulnerable psychiatric populations.

title: Is loss of antidepressant effect during continuation therapy related to placebo effect?

screening.rationale: No abstract or full-text provided; title suggests a placebo-related question but available record is insufficient to judge whether placebo/nocebo effects were the study's explicit focus or merely a comparator.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title asked whether loss of antidepressant effect during continuation therapy was related to the placebo effect, but methods and results were not provided in the record.

title: Methods and models for placebo use in pharmacotherapeutic trials.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a review of methods and models for placebo use in pharmacotherapeutic trials, so placebo science/methodology is the explicit focus (review).

classification.summary: Reviewed methodological approaches and models for using placebos in pharmacotherapy trials and discussed trial-design implications for placebo use.

title: Predictors of placebo response in depression.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly states the paper's focus is on predictors of placebo response in depression, meeting inclusion criterion 2 (placebo response as the object of study), despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Reviews predictors of placebo response in depression, synthesizing factors associated with improvement in placebo arms of antidepressant trials.

title: A comparative study of continuous ultrasound, placebo ultrasound and rest in epicondylalgia.
abstract: In this study the pain alleviating effects of continuous ultrasound treatment in epicondylalgia has been compared to placebo ultrasound and to rest. Of 99 patients 33 were randomly allocated to receive continuous ultrasound treatment, 33 to placebo ultrasound treatment and 33 were recommended only rest. The 66 patients treated were each given 10 treatments over 5 to 6 weeks. The condition was significantly improved in the group treated with continuous ultrasound in 36%, in 30% given placebo, and in 24% of those recommended rest. A significant improvement was noted when the effect of continuous ultrasound was compared with rest, but continuous ultrasound treatment was not significantly better than placebo ultrasound.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial directly compared placebo (sham) ultrasound to rest, isolating a placebo/context effect versus no-treatment and reporting placebo-arm response.

classification.summary: Randomized trial in 99 patients with epicondylalgia compared continuous ultrasound, placebo (sham) ultrasound, and rest, and reported improvement rates of 36% (continuous), 30% (placebo), and 24% (rest); continuous was superior to rest but not to placebo.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (sham) ultrasound produced a 30% improvement rate versus 24% with rest, and continuous ultrasound (36%) did not differ significantly from placebo.

title: Placebo challenge: effects following repeated alcohol vs. placebo administration.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title and MeSH imply a placebo/challenge experiment with alcohol but available information is insufficient to confirm that placebo/nocebo phenomena were the explicit primary focus.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to determine focus; title and MeSH suggest an experimental placebo-challenge comparing repeated alcohol versus placebo with conditioning and physiological measures.

title: The methodological and clinical aspects of the placebo effect in angina pectoris.
abstract: The study was carried out in 45 patients (36 males and 9 females) experiencing more attacks on the evaluation of an antianginal drug in a placebo-controlled trial, and to define some conditions of placebo sensitiveness in patients with angina pectoris. The study was carried out in 45 patients (36 males and 9 females) experiencing more than 5 anginal attacks a week. The drug compared with the placebo was Iso-Mack-Retard 20 believed to have a good antianginal profile. The efficacy of both the drug and placebo was assessed mainly by the number of anginal attacks per week. The differences in the efficacy between the drug and its placebo in the group studied as a whole were not statistically significant but, after exclusion of 15 placebo-sensitive patients (placebo responders), these differences increased to become statistically significant (p less than 0.01). Moreover, the study proved that the extent of the placebo effect in a population is inversely dependent on the level of neuroticism measured by Eysenck Personality Inventory, and directly dependent on the number of anginal attacks in the period before administration of the drug.

screening.rationale: Placebo responsiveness was an explicit study focus (identifying 'placebo-sensitive' patients and predictors) and the paper analyzed placebo-arm responses in an angina RCT.

classification.summary: Studied 45 patients with frequent angina in a placebo-controlled trial and identified placebo-sensitive patients; placebo response magnitude related to lower neuroticism and greater baseline attack frequency.
classification.key_finding: Excluding 15 placebo-responsive patients made drug-versus-placebo differences significant (p<0.01), and placebo effect size was inversely related to Eysenck neuroticism and directly related to baseline attack frequency.

title: Efficacy and duration of action of placebo responses in the prevention of exercise-induced asthma in children.
journal: The Journal of asthma : official journal of the Association for the Care of Asthma
abstract: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, a common phenomenon in asthmatic children, may be prevented by the administration of appropriate drugs. In this study we evaluated the effect and duration of action of placebo (Freon gasses) administered to the patients as a protective drug. The maximum decrease in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) after exercise testing was 40.3% +/- 3.10 at the initial screening session and, on different study days, 23.3% +/- 3.57, 28.8% +/- 3.86, and 33.7% +/- 3.71 30, 120, and 240 minutes, respectively, after the administration of Freon gasses. There was a linear trend indicating a reduction in protection with time. The placebo effect was marked 30-120 minutes after treatment (p less than 0.01) and completely disappeared after 4 hours. The placebo effect should always be considered in the evaluation of any new antiasthmatic drug.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly measured the magnitude and duration of a placebo intervention (inhaled 'Freon' gas) on exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in children, making placebo response the object of study.

classification.summary: Measured the protective effect and time course of an inhaled placebo (Freon gas) against exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in asthmatic children and found significant bronchoprotection at 30–120 minutes that disappeared by 4 hours.
classification.key_finding: Placebo inhalation produced significant objective improvement in FEV1 protection at 30–120 minutes post-administration (p<0.01), which declined linearly and was absent at 4 hours.

title: The use of placebo trials as part of a forensic assessment.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper's main subject is the use of placebo trials in forensic assessment (ethical/practical discussion), meeting placebo_science_other inclusion for placebo-focused commentary.

classification.summary: Discussed ethical, legal, and practical issues of using placebo trials during forensic psychiatric assessments.

title: Expectancy effects on respiration during lactate infusion.
abstract: The effect of lactate infusion on pCO2 and respiration rate was studied in two differently instructed groups of healthy volunteers in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over study. Both groups showed a significant decrease in alveolar pCO2 after lactate but not after placebo. This was accompanied by an increase in respiration rate in those subjects who had expected to become anxious and by a decrease in respiration rate in those who had expected to experience pleasant excitement.

screening.rationale: The study experimentally manipulated expectancy (verbal instruction) in a placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover lactate/placebo infusion, and tested respiratory physiological responses as a function of expectation, making placebo/nocebo mechanisms the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Manipulated expectations in a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover lactate/placebo infusion and found lactate reduced pCO2, while respiration rate changed differently depending on whether subjects expected anxiety or pleasant excitement.
classification.key_finding: Lactate decreased alveolar pCO2, and respiration rate increased with anxiety expectancy but decreased with pleasant-excitement expectancy, indicating expectancy modulated physiological respiratory responses.

title: Heart rate and blood pressure during placebo-associated panic attacks.
abstract: Increases in the anxiety ratings, heart rate, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure were compared in eight panicking and 57 nonpanicking panic disorder patients during placebo (dextrose) infusions. Heart rate and systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased significantly in placebo-infused panickers, but these increases did not correlate well with increases in anxiety.

screening.rationale: The study empirically examined adverse responses (panic, HR/BP increases) occurring during a placebo (dextrose) infusion, making placebo/nocebo phenomena the study focus (nocebo response).

classification.summary: Compared anxiety ratings, heart rate, and blood pressure during placebo (dextrose) infusions and found that panicking patients showed significant increases in anxiety and cardiovascular measures during the placebo infusion.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (dextrose) infusion triggered panic with significant increases in heart rate and systolic/diastolic blood pressure in panicking patients (n=8), though physiological increases did not correlate well with anxiety ratings.

title: Hypnosis, placebo, and suggestion in the treatment of warts.
abstract: Two experiments assessed the effects of psychological variables on wart regression. In Experiment 1, subjects given hypnotic suggestion exhibited more wart regression than those given either a placebo treatment or no treatment. In Experiment 2, hypnotic and nonhypnotic subjects given the same suggestions were equally likely to exhibit wart regression and more likely to show this effect than no treatment controls. In both experiments, treated subjects who lost warts reported more vivid suggested imagery than treated subjects who did not lose warts. However, hypnotizability and attribute measures of imagery propensity were unrelated to wart loss. Subjects given the suggestion that they would lose warts on only one side of the body did not show evidence of a side-specific treatment effect.

screening.rationale: Experiments manipulated suggestion/hypnosis and compared treated (placebo or suggestion) versus no-treatment controls, with wart regression as the primary outcome (placebo/nocebo phenomena explicitly tested).

classification.summary: Conducted two experiments showing hypnotic or suggested imagery produced greater wart regression than no treatment, and suggestion without hypnosis worked similarly to hypnosis.
classification.key_finding: Found that suggestion-driven imagery (with or without hypnosis) increased wart regression relative to no-treatment controls; hypnotizability did not predict outcome.

title: Effects of alcohol conditioning and expectancy on a visuo-motor integration task.
abstract: Two experiments were performed in which the classical conditioning model of tolerance, the habituation theory of tolerance, and state dependent learning theory made conflicting predictions. In the first experiment, alcohol conditioning did not produce a compensatory response under placebo on a visuo-motor integration task, but disguised alcohol produced a large decrement in performance. Since the results were consistent both with habituation and state dependent learning theories, a second experiment was performed in which all subjects received alcohol, but half were told that they were receiving pure tonic water. The finding of no expectancy effect was inconsistent with habituation theory, but fully consistent with state dependent learning theory.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated expectancy (told tonic water vs. alcohol) and tested conditioned/placebo responses to alcohol on visuo-motor performance, making placebo/expectancy phenomena a primary focus.

classification.summary: Tested alcohol conditioning and expectancy effects on visuo-motor performance; found no compensatory placebo response but impaired performance with disguised alcohol, and no expectancy effect when subjects were told they received tonic water.
classification.key_finding: Conditioning did not produce compensatory placebo effects; disguised alcohol impaired performance; explicit expectancy manipulation produced no effect, supporting state-dependent learning over habituation.

title: Placebo injections and surveillance of alcohol intake during inpatient treatment of female alcoholics.
abstract: Institutions for treating alcoholics differ widely with respect to how restrictively they apply psychopharmacological agents and how rigorously they control patients for intake of alcohol. This study investigates the impact of such policies on relapse rates. During a three month inpatient treatment, 70 female alcoholics were assigned to one of four conditions: (a) strict surveillance of alcohol intake by means of breath tests and frequent checks of patient's rooms as well as injections of a placebo purportedly reducing craving, (b) no surveillance but placebo injections, (c) surveillance but no placebo injections, and (d) neither surveillance nor placebo injections. The amount of surveillance did not influence relapse rates. However, during inpatient treatment more relapses occurred among patients who received the placebo injections than among those who did not. Although this effect was no longer significant following treatment, the increase of relapse rates suggests caution in the application of nonspecific medication in the treatment of alcoholics.

screening.rationale: Randomized inpatient trial explicitly manipulated placebo injections versus no injections and measured relapse rates, making placebo/nocebo phenomena the study's focus.

classification.summary: Randomized trial of 70 female inpatients tested placebo injections and surveillance policies and found more relapses during treatment among those who received placebo injections.
classification.key_finding: Placebo injections purported to reduce craving were associated with a higher relapse rate during inpatient treatment.

title: Placebo response rates in psychotic and nonpsychotic depression.
abstract: The authors reanalyzed data from two earlier studies that used double-blind placebo-controlled formats to study the efficacy of amitriptyline. Using a 14-day drug-free 'wash-out' period, they found that the placebo response rates were 0% for psychotic depressives and 13.3% for nonpsychotic depressives. Amitriptyline was significantly superior to placebo for both psychotic (P less than or equal to 0.05) and nonpsychotic (P less than or equal to 0.05) depressed patients.

screening.rationale: Paper reanalyzed placebo-controlled trials with the explicit analytic focus on placebo response rates in psychotic versus nonpsychotic depression (placebo-arm analysis).

classification.summary: Reanalyzed two double-blind amitriptyline trials and reported placebo response rates of 0% in psychotic depression and 13.3% in nonpsychotic depression.
classification.key_finding: Placebo response rates were 0% for psychotic depressives and 13.3% for nonpsychotic depressives.

title: Reduction of post-operative swelling by a placebo effect.
abstract: A placebo effect on post-operative swelling was investigated as a possible model for studying psychological influences on recovery from surgery. 79 patients undergoing removal of impacted third-molars received one of five different procedures shortly after emerging from general anaesthetic. These included dentist-administered or placebo ultrasound (the latter given in two different ways to control for massage effects), untreated controls and a group instructed to apply facial massage to themselves. Pre- and post-operative measurements included trait and state-anxiety, coping style, emotional state, pain, plasma cortisol and facial swelling. Cortisol levels correlated with anxiety and avoidant coping. Post-operative anxiety was negatively correlated with pre-operative arousal. Neither coping nor emotional state was affected by the treatments, but swelling was reduced by a placebo effect of ultrasound. Cortisol levels also responded, apparently to an effect of massage. The coping and emotional factors which we measured here cannot, therefore, explain the effects of this psychological procedure on post-operative recovery.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled comparison including placebo (sham) ultrasound versus untreated controls tested placebo effects on post-operative swelling, making placebo the explicit object of study.

classification.summary: Compared sham ultrasound, active massage, and untreated controls after third-molar extraction and found that placebo (sham) ultrasound reduced post-operative facial swelling and cortisol varied with massage.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (sham) ultrasound produced a measurable reduction in post-operative swelling compared with untreated controls.

title: Characterization of the associative nature of sensitization to amphetamine-induced circling behavior and of the environment dependent placebo-like response.
abstract: Amphetamine-induced circling behavior increases over the course of repeated administration of the drug; likewise, after repeated administration of amphetamine, an injection of saline prior to placement of the rat in the test apparatus previously associated with the pharmacologic effects of amphetamine will increase circling behavior. Experiments were designed to determine if either of these effects would respond to manipulation of the temporal contiguity between the test environment and the peak effects of amphetamine. The placebo-like response, in accordance with a Pavlovian conditioned response, was reduced by prior non-reinforced exposure to the test environment and subject to extinction. In contrast, the increase in the amphetamine-induced response was entirely dependent on the test environment but not affected by latent inhibition or extinction. These and previous findings indicate that the development and expression of the placebo-like response is the result of a Pavlovian associative process. Although amphetamine sensitization is environment dependent, it does not resemble a conditioned response in other respects.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment explicitly studied a Pavlovian 'placebo-like' saline response to a drug-paired environment (placebo response/conditioning was the paper's focus).

classification.summary: Found that saline given before placement in a drug-paired environment produced conditioned increases in amphetamine-like circling behavior that were reduced by nonreinforced exposure and extinction, while amphetamine sensitization was environment-dependent but not extinguished.
classification.key_finding: Saline injections in the amphetamine-paired environment produced a conditioned, placebo-like increase in circling that was subject to latent inhibition and extinction.
